clue.text: A loveless attitude in part of church?

indicators.note: love is zero in tennis scores, the round letter, so 'loveless' tells you to drop that letter from the attitude word

blocks.note: the article kept as it is
POSE (an attitude struck) with its O removed

explanation.surface: A cold, unloving mood hanging about some corner of a church.
explanation.walkthrough: Love is O, from the zero score in tennis. The question mark admits the definition is loose: an APSE is one particular part of a church.
explanation.definitionFit: An apse is the rounded, vaulted recess at the east end of a church building, so it is literally one section of it.

clue.text: Hate a man being nasty, much disliked person

indicators.note: letters that turn nasty misbehave and fall out of their proper order

explanation.surface: Someone loathes a spiteful man, a person nobody can stand.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as one long sentence about hatred, but the first three words are only letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Anathema names something or someone intensely detested, as in 'he is anathema to them', a common idiomatic use.

clue.text: Mock one rebel, having posed first

indicators.note: the posing word is told to go at the front, ahead of one and the rebel

blocks.note: sat for a portrait, as a model poses

explanation.surface: Jeering at an insurgent who once modelled for an artist.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue lists one and rebel before posed, but 'having posed first' moves SAT to the front of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To satirise is to ridicule a target through humour or exaggeration, a straightforward synonym for mock as a verb.

clue.text: Juice oozed and maybe went to the ground

blocks.note: stum is unfermented grape juice, a crossword staple
leaked out slowly, as blood or dye does

explanation.surface: Liquid seeped out and perhaps soaked into the soil.
explanation.walkthrough: STUM, grape must before fermentation, is rare outside crosswords. 'Maybe' marks the definition as an example: someone who stumbled may or may not have hit the ground.
explanation.definitionFit: Tripping often ends in a fall, so a person who tripped perhaps finished lying on the floor, hence the hedge.

clue.text: Mark the man who provides such reliable evidence?

definitions.text: Mark the man who provides such reliable evidence?

blocks.note: surface: pay attention to this fellow, a trustworthy witness

blocks.clueFragment: Mark the man who provides such reliable evidence?
blocks.note: setter's reading: Mark is the evangelist, whose account of Jesus is one of the four books of the New Testament

explanation.walkthrough: 'Mark' looks like a verb meaning note; it is the name of the evangelist Saint Mark, author of the second book of the New Testament.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is an idiom for something completely true, the evangelists' accounts being held as unquestionable by believers.

clue.text: Ambition rising, I'm turning up in American city

indicators.note: in a down clue something rising reads from bottom to top, so ambition goes backwards
turning upward in a down entry flips the order of the letters in I'm

blocks.note: an aim is a goal or ambition
taken as printed, without the apostrophe

explanation.surface: A hopeful person arriving to seek their fortune in a US city.
explanation.walkthrough: Both pieces are reversed separately, then set side by side.
explanation.definitionFit: Miami is a large city on the Florida coast of the United States, so it is one example of a US metropolis.

clue.text: Communication in character from landlord

blocks.note: a written message sent by post
a single symbol of the alphabet

explanation.walkthrough: Three senses, not two: 'in' and 'from' just join them. The landlord sense is a crossword favourite, one who lets.
explanation.definitionFit: A letter is posted correspondence, an alphabet symbol, and jokily a person who rents rooms or houses out to tenants.

clue.text: Compulsion of the upper classes to appear in finery?

indicators.note: the upper classes are shown dressed up inside the finery, so their letter sits within it

blocks.note: U is the old label for upper-class usage
fine clothes, as in full dress

explanation.surface: The pressure on the gentry always to turn up in their best clothes.
explanation.walkthrough: U for upper class comes from Nancy Mitford's 'U and non-U' labels for posh and common speech.
explanation.definitionFit: Duress means threats or pressure forcing someone to act against their will, the same idea as being compelled.

clue.text: County ramble going in direction of gale

blocks.note: to wind is to meander, as a rambling path does

explanation.surface: A country walk heading the way a storm is blowing.
explanation.walkthrough: DOWN is one of the six counties of Northern Ireland. 'Ramble' suggests a walk, but here it is the verb for wandering off course.
explanation.definitionFit: Downwind describes moving the same way as the blowing air, carried along with a strong breeze behind.

clue.text: One with false tears I observed in place in parliament expressing condolences

indicators.note: false tears are not the real thing, so the word is a counterfeit arrangement of its letters
the pieces are seen inside the parliamentary place, so they sit within it

blocks.note: the House of Commons, the lower chamber

explanation.surface: A crocodile-tears politician sitting in the House, offering sympathy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Place in parliament' is the House of Commons, the elected lower chamber of the UK Parliament; everything before 'observed' sits inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Commiserations are expressions of sympathy for someone's loss or misfortune, close synonyms of the plural noun.

clue.text: Endless wine with party in Italian city stadium

indicators.note: a word without an end has lost its last letter, so the wine is cut short
the party is placed inside the name of the Italian city

blocks.note: ASTI, the sparkling Piedmont wine, minus its final letter
a do is a party or celebration

explanation.surface: Drinking bottomless wine at a party in an Italian city's arena.
explanation.walkthrough: AST then RO(DO)ME. The Astrodome in Houston was the first domed sports stadium.
explanation.definitionFit: The Astrodome is a famous covered sports arena in Texas, a specific example of the general word.

clue.text: Nonsense about retiring player

indicators.note: retiring means withdrawing or going back, so the letters run backwards

explanation.surface: Silly talk surrounding a sportsman hanging up his boots.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Retiring player' reads as one phrase about a sportsman, but 'retiring' belongs to the wordplay and 'player' stands alone as the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A player in the theatrical sense is a performer on stage, an old but standard synonym.

clue.text: Flier restricted by weather once

indicators.note: the answer is hemmed in by the surrounding words, kept inside their letters

blocks.note: found across the join of the two words

explanation.surface: A plane grounded by bad weather in times past.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flier' suggests an aircraft or a pilot, which suits the weather; it is a bird.
explanation.definitionFit: A heron is a long-legged wading bird, and any bird is something that travels through the air.

clue.text: Gloomy feeling, low, eats heart of loser

blocks.note: the central letter of the five

explanation.surface: A beaten competitor, down in the dumps, comfort eating.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Low' looks like it means sad, fitting the gloom; it is the noise a cow makes.
explanation.definitionFit: Moodiness is a tendency to sulky, sullen spirits, a state of mind close to melancholy.

clue.text: Girl is very good about drink – there's a lot of water in it

definitions.text: there's a lot of water in it

indicators.note: here the word means concerning, so the good word is attached next to the drink

blocks.note: pious, crossword shorthand for very good

explanation.surface: A well-behaved young woman sipping, with plenty of water in her glass.
explanation.walkthrough: PI (pious) for 'very good' is a crossword convention. The definition is cryptic: a great river certainly has a lot of water in it.
explanation.definitionFit: The Mississippi is one of the longest rivers in North America, carrying an enormous volume of flow.

clue.text: Disposed to be at home – a hundred and wrinkled

explanation.surface: A centenarian, creased with age, content to stay in.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface paints an old person at home, which makes 'a hundred' read as an age; it is just C.
explanation.definitionFit: Being inclined to do something means having a tendency or leaning toward it, the same as being disposed.

clue.text: What could baffle e.g. dim man?

definitions.text: What could baffle e.g. dim man?

indicators.note: a baffled mind is confused, so the letters that follow are jumbled up

explanation.surface: Asking what might confuse a slow-witted fellow.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue does double duty: the letters of 'e.g. dim man' jumbled give the answer, and the whole sentence describes it.
explanation.definitionFit: A mind game is psychological manipulation intended to confuse or unsettle someone, exactly something that could bewilder a dull person.

clue.text: Soldiers perhaps around hostile eastern islands

indicators.note: the soldiers stand on both sides of hostile and eastern, enclosing them

blocks.note: soldier ants are one caste, so soldiers are an example of ants

explanation.surface: Troops surrounding unfriendly islands in the east.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Soldiers' suggests troops, fitting 'hostile'; 'perhaps' warns they are only an example, here insects.
explanation.definitionFit: The Antilles are the island chain of the Caribbean, split into the Greater and Lesser groups.

clue.text: Remissness from priest taken in by dodgy doctrine

indicators.note: something dodgy is unreliable and suspect, so the doctrine is not in its proper order
the priest is absorbed inside the scrambled doctrine

blocks.note: Eli, the priest who raised Samuel in the Old Testament

explanation.surface: A cleric duped by a questionable creed and so neglecting his duties.
explanation.walkthrough: ELI is the standard crossword priest, from the Book of Samuel.
explanation.definitionFit: Dereliction, as in dereliction of duty, is shameful neglect of what one ought to do, the same as remissness.

clue.text: Explosive Conservative – Conservative almost becoming bully

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the second party word loses its last letter

explanation.surface: A hot-tempered right-winger turning into a thug.
explanation.walkthrough: A Tory is a member of the UK Conservative Party. 'Explosive' looks like an adjective for a temper; it is the noun, HE.
explanation.definitionFit: To hector is to browbeat or intimidate with loud talk, and as a noun a hector is a blustering tormentor.

clue.text: Cry from cats finally getting best milk

indicators.note: the end of cats gets, or acquires, the milk word, so they are put side by side

blocks.note: the final letter of the word
the richest part of milk, rising to the top

explanation.surface: Cats yowling until they are given the richest milk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Getting' just joins the two pieces, the letter taking on the dairy word.
explanation.definitionFit: A scream is a loud piercing shriek, one kind of vocal outburst, matching the noun sense of the definition.

clue.text: Meet bridge opponents in front of bar

indicators.note: the opponents are placed ahead of the bar, one after the other

blocks.note: East and North, who play against each other at bridge
the serving counter in a pub or shop

explanation.surface: Card players arranging to see each other ahead of a trip to the pub.
explanation.walkthrough: In bridge, North and South are partners against East and West, so any E paired with N or S makes opponents.
explanation.definitionFit: To encounter someone is to come upon or face them, a straightforward verb synonym for meeting.

clue.text: Ahead, prepared for trouble

blocks.note: leading, as in two goals up

explanation.surface: Out in front and braced for a fight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Prepared for trouble' reads as one phrase; the break comes after 'prepared'.
explanation.definitionFit: To upset people is to disturb or distress them, the same verb sense as to trouble someone.

clue.text: Animal caught in rain, dripping

indicators.note: the answer is trapped within the words that follow, spanning their join

explanation.surface: A creature stuck out in a downpour, soaked through.
explanation.walkthrough: The INDRI is a large lemur of Madagascar, a word met mostly in crosswords.
explanation.definitionFit: The indri is a mammal, the biggest living lemur, so it is one example of a creature.

clue.text: Tension, missing opening? It's hairy

indicators.note: the word for tension lacks its start, so its first letter goes

explanation.surface: Someone nervous before a first night, feeling things are getting fraught.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It's hairy' sounds like slang for 'it's scary', matching the tension; read literally, it is a thing made of hair.
explanation.definitionFit: A tress is a long lock of human hair, so it is literally composed entirely of strands from the head.

clue.text: What bowler needs joining cricket side – to be alert

indicators.note: one thing joining another is attached to it, so the pieces sit together

blocks.note: the on side, the leg side of the field
a bowler cannot bowl without it

explanation.surface: A cricket bowler joining the team needs to keep sharp.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket the on side is the half of the field behind the batter's legs. The first phrase is a mini cryptic definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Being on the ball is an idiom for being quick-witted and aware of what is going on.

clue.text: More unusual ordeal, most unfriendly in manner

indicators.note: an unusual version of the word is out of the ordinary, rearranged

explanation.surface: A stranger, tougher trial from the coldest of hosts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'More unusual' reads as a comparative adjective, but 'More' is the fodder and 'unusual' the instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: A remote person is aloof and distant, so the superlative describes the coldest, least approachable demeanour.

clue.text: Confusion in words transmitted, short of time

indicators.note: being short of something means lacking it, so the time word is removed

explanation.surface: A garbled radio message cut off before its time.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove AGE from MESSAGE to leave the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A mess is a state of disorder or muddle, a common everyday synonym for a confused situation.
